balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue mix
segmentRevenue.content:
Corpay reports three operating segments plus an Other bucket: Vehicle Payments (fuel cards, Brazilian electronic tolling/Sem Parar, EV charging, vehicle compliance), Corporate Payments (AP automation, cross-border FX/payments, virtual and purchasing cards) and Lodging Payments (discounted corporate/airline/insurance hotel bookings); Other covers gift cards, payroll cards and outsourced card processing.

For Corpay: Corporate Payments (~41% of revenue) is compounding at 30-40%+ reported growth on Alpha Group, GPS Capital Markets and AvidXchange M&A, overtaking Vehicle Payments (~43%, still the largest segment but structurally pressured by the EV transition and fuel-price/spread volatility) as the growth engine. A Q1-2026 segment realignment moved outsourced card processing into Other and spend-management enterprise clients into Corporate Payments, so the FY2025-to-FY2026 step is a reporting break, not organic acceleration.

What to watch:

  • Corporate Payments' share of total revenue rising as the re-rating thesis (payments-platform multiple vs. legacy fuel-card multiple)
  • Vehicle Payments holding flat-to-growing in absolute dollars even as its share shrinks
  • Lodging and Other staying small enough not to matter to the thesis either way

segmentOrganicGrowth.title: Organic revenue growth by segment
segmentOrganicGrowth.content:
Organic growth strips out the effect of acquisitions and divestitures (Alpha, AvidXchange, GPS, Paymerang, Gringo on the buy side; PayByPhone, UK Maintenance, the BP fuel-card portfolio on the sell side) to show underlying volume and pricing trends within each segment.

For Corpay: Corporate Payments' organic growth (high-teens%) run well ahead of Vehicle Payments' (mid-single-digits%) is the organic half of the re-rating case -- the M&A-driven reported-revenue mix shift in the chart above is not the whole story. Lodging has run negative in several recent periods.

What to watch:

  • Corporate Payments organic growth decelerating toward Vehicle Payments' rate (the M&A premium thesis weakening)
  • Vehicle Payments organic growth turning negative (EV transition biting faster than priced in)
  • Lodging's persistent softness versus the other three segments

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Corpay, Inc. (formerly FleetCor Technologies, Inc.): the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
